items.title: L12: Compound logic with AND, OR and NOT
items.source: Microsoft Support: AND, OR, NOT and IF functions
items.body:
Real rules combine several conditions. A rule might read: =IF(AND(B2>=18,OR(C2="UK",C2="IE"),NOT(D2="Yes")),"Eligible","Refer"). B2 is age, C2 is country and D2 is a flag for a previous refusal. AND returns TRUE only if every condition is TRUE. OR returns TRUE if at least one is. NOT reverses a result. Four rows show the effect. Age 17, UK, No gives Refer, because the age test fails. Age 18, IE, No gives Eligible. Age 30, FR, No gives Refer, because the country test fails. Age 40, UK, Yes gives Refer, because NOT(D2="Yes") is FALSE. Text comparisons are not case-sensitive, so "uk" matches "UK".

Two points catch people out. First, AND and OR do not stop early. AND(A2<>0,10/A2>1) still works out the second test when A2 is 0, and returns #DIV/0!. IF does choose between its branches, so =IF(A2=0,"",10/A2) is safe. Second, an empty B2 counts as 0, so B2>=18 is FALSE and the row is sent to Refer, which may be right for the wrong reason. Test for blanks explicitly if missing data should be reported differently.

NOT(AND(x,y)) is the same as OR(NOT(x),NOT(y)), and NOT(OR(x,y)) is the same as AND(NOT(x),NOT(y)). Use whichever is easier to read. When the rule is for a policy decision, put each condition in its own labelled column, so that a reviewer can see which test failed. The final formula then simply combines the TRUE or FALSE flags. Test every boundary: age exactly 18, age 17, and each country.

items.title: L12: Lookup keys: data types, spaces and duplicates
items.source: Microsoft Support: XLOOKUP, MATCH, COUNTIF and TRIM functions
items.body:
Most lookup failures come from keys that look the same but are not. The commonest is a data type mismatch. A reference of 1001 stored as a number will not match "1001" stored as text, so VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP and MATCH all return #N/A. Left-aligned numbers are a clue that they are text. COUNTIF behaves differently: it treats 1001 and "1001" as the same, so COUNTIF can say the key exists while XLOOKUP says it does not.

The second cause is hidden spaces. TRIM removes leading and trailing spaces and reduces runs of spaces between words to one. It does not remove non-breaking spaces, which often arrive in data copied from web pages. Those are character 160, and =SUBSTITUTE(A2,CHAR(160)," ") replaces them with ordinary spaces. LEN is a quick test: if LEN(A2) is larger than the number of characters you can see, something is hidden.

Duplicates cause quieter errors. When a key appears more than once, VLOOKUP, MATCH and XLOOKUP return the first match. With XLOOKUP, search_mode -1 searches from the last item to the first and returns the last match. Check for duplicates with =COUNTIF(A:A,A2)>1, and decide which record is correct before you look anything up.

XLOOKUP can use wildcards if match_mode is 2. In that mode, an asterisk stands for any number of characters and a question mark for exactly one. So "Sm*" would match "Smith" and "Smythe". A tilde before a wildcard character, as in ~*, searches for the actual symbol. Exact-match lookups ignore case.

Fix the data, not the formula. Clean keys in a helper column using TRIM and VALUE, and look up on that column. Never turn off the error handling to make a lookup appear to work.

items.title: L12: Weighted scoring and ranking with SUMPRODUCT
items.source: Microsoft Support: SUMPRODUCT, RANK.EQ and COUNTIF functions
items.body:
Evaluating options against weighted criteria is a routine job. Four candidates, A to D, are scored out of 100 against three criteria weighted 50%, 30% and 20%. The scores are: A 80, 70, 60; B 90, 60, 50; C 70, 90, 80; D 85, 65, 75. For each candidate, =SUMPRODUCT(weights,scores) multiplies each score by its weight and adds them. The totals are A 73, B 73, C 78 and D 77. The ranking is therefore C first, D second, and A and B tied on 73.

Check that the weights add up to 100%, with a cell such as =SUM(weights)=1. The arrays in SUMPRODUCT must be the same shape. If the weights run across a row and the scores down a column, the formula returns #VALUE!.

RANK.EQ gives tied scores the same rank and skips the next number. A and B both rank 3 and nothing ranks 4. To break ties with a clear rule, add a counter: =RANK.EQ(E2,$E$2:$E$5)+COUNTIF($E$2:E2,E2)-1. That gives A rank 3 and B rank 4, by order in the list. The tiebreak is arbitrary, so a better method is to apply an agreed second criterion, such as the highest score on the most important criterion.

Test how sensitive the result is to the weights. If the weights are changed to 20%, 30% and 50%, the totals become A 67, B 61, C 81 and D 74. The order is still C, D, A and B, but the gaps differ. When a decision flips on a small change to the weights, say so in the paper. Agree the weights before you see the scores, otherwise they can be bent to fit a preferred outcome.

questions.hint: Fixing weights first keeps the process fair.

items.title: L12: Dates: financial years and quarters
items.source: HMRC and GOV.UK: UK tax year and financial year; Microsoft Support: date functions
items.body:
Government finance works on a financial year from 1 April to 31 March. A date in February 2025 belongs to the 2024-25 year. Excel has no built-in function for this, so you build it from YEAR and MONTH. The year in which the financial year starts is =YEAR(A2)-(MONTH(A2)<4). The comparison returns TRUE (1) when the month is January to March, so one is subtracted. For 15 February 2025 this gives 2024, and for 1 April 2025 it gives 2025.

The financial quarter is =INT(MOD(MONTH(A2)-4,12)/3)+1. Quarter 1 is April to June, Quarter 2 is July to September, Quarter 3 is October to December and Quarter 4 is January to March. February gives MOD(-2,12) = 10, then 10/3 = 3.33, INT gives 3, plus 1 is Quarter 4. October gives 6/3 = 2, so Quarter 3. MOD returns a positive result here because it takes the sign of the divisor.

To count the days remaining in the financial year, subtract the date from the final day: =DATE(start_year+1,3,31)-A2. From 15 February 2025 this gives 44 days.

Watch for leap years. DATE(2025,2,29) does not give an error. It overflows to 1 March 2025. February 2024 had 29 days. EDATE and EOMONTH handle month lengths correctly, so use them rather than adding 30.

Dates imported from other systems can be read the wrong way round. A text date such as 03/04/2025 may be 3 April in the UK but 4 March in the US format. Check a few rows where the day is above 12, such as 25/04/2025, since those can only be read one way. Store dates as real dates, and format them clearly, for instance 3 April 2025.

items.title: L12: Spreadsheet controls: tables, assumptions and protection
items.source: HM Treasury: Review of quality assurance of government analytical models (Macpherson Review); AQuA Book; Microsoft Support
items.body:
Spreadsheets that inform decisions need controls. The Macpherson review of government models and the AQuA Book both stress structure, documentation, checking and accountability. A manager does not need to build the formulas but should expect these features.

Separate the sheet into inputs, calculations and outputs. Put every assumption, such as a rate or a date, in one labelled cell and refer to it. A formula such as =B2*1.2 hides the 20% in the formula; if the rate changes you have to find every copy of it. Use =B2*(1+VATRate) instead. Colour or label input cells consistently and say what the colours mean.

Excel Tables, created with Ctrl+T, extend automatically and allow structured references such as Table1[Cost], which are easier to read than C2:C500 and do not miss new rows. Named ranges give meaningful labels to key cells.

Add checks. A reconciliation cell compares a total with an independent figure, for example =ROUND(SUM(Detail[Cost])-Summary!B2,2)=0. A single overall check cell on the front sheet should show any failed test. Keep an explanatory sheet: purpose, owner, version, source of data, assumptions and known limits.

Protection stops accidental overwriting but is not security. A sheet-protection password is easy to remove, and hidden sheets can be unhidden. For sensitive content use encrypted storage and access controls. Before sharing, remove hidden data and comments. Use clear version names, record who reviewed the model, and keep the reviewed version read-only. Avoid links to other workbooks where possible, since they break when files move. Check that calculation mode is automatic; in manual mode figures may be out of date.

items.title: L12: Cleaning text data with functions
items.source: Microsoft Support: TRIM, MID, FIND, SUBSTITUTE, TEXT and TEXTJOIN functions
items.body:
Case references often arrive as one block of text. Suppose A2 holds "  CASE-2025-0042  " with two spaces at each end. LEN(A2) is 18, while LEN(TRIM(A2)) is 14, since TRIM removes the extra spaces. The clean reference is CASE-2025-0042.

MID extracts text from the middle: =MID(TRIM(A2),6,4) starts at the sixth character and takes four, giving "2025". RIGHT(TRIM(A2),4) gives "0042" as text. Wrap it in VALUE and you get the number 42. FIND returns the position of one string in another and is case-sensitive: FIND("-",TRIM(A2)) returns 5. SEARCH is similar but not case-sensitive, and allows wildcards. SUBSTITUTE swaps specified text: SUBSTITUTE(TRIM(A2),"-","") returns "CASE20250042".

To bring back leading zeros, use TEXT: =TEXT(42,"0000") returns "0042". The result is text, so it cannot be relied on for numbers in later calculations. TEXT is also used for display, for example =TEXT(0.256,"0.0%") gives "25.6%" and =TEXT(A2,"d mmmm yyyy") shows a date in words. Build the display text in a separate cell from the underlying number.

TEXTJOIN joins items with a separator and can skip empty cells: =TEXTJOIN(", ",TRUE,A2:A5) joins four cells, leaving out blanks. PROPER capitalises each word, but is not reliable for names: "mcdonald" becomes "Mcdonald". CLEAN removes non-printing characters. After cleaning with formulas, copy and paste as values into a new column and keep the original.

Test cleaning formulas on awkward rows, such as short entries, entries with no hyphen and entries with extra spaces, since a formula that works on one row may fail on another.

items.title: L12: Options appraisal: weighing options and discounting
items.source: HM Treasury: The Green Book; Business case guidance (five case model)
items.body:
A submission with options must compare like with like. HM Treasury's Green Book sets the standard for appraising proposals. Options should include a "do nothing" or "business as usual" baseline, so that the benefit of each alternative is measured against what would happen anyway. A long list of options is narrowed to a shortlist against the objectives and critical success factors.

Business cases use five dimensions, often called the five case model: strategic (is there a case for change), economic (value for money), commercial (can it be procured), financial (is it affordable) and management (can it be delivered). A submission to a minister does not repeat the whole business case but should tell the reader which of these dimensions is weak.

Costs and benefits arising at different times are discounted, since a pound today is worth more than a pound in future. The Green Book's standard rate is 3.5 per cent a year. The present value of £100 received in one year is 100 divided by 1.035, or £96.62. In two years it is 100 divided by 1.035 squared, £93.35. The present value of £100 in each of the next three years is £280.16, which is less than £300. Costs in future years are discounted in the same way. Compare options on net present value, and also on whether they can be afforded in the budget year.

Appraisal also deals with risk and optimism bias. Early estimates of cost and time are often too low, so the Green Book asks for an uplift or an adjustment that is reduced as evidence improves. Show sensitivity: say what happens if costs rise by 20 per cent or benefits arrive late. A good submission states the preferred option, the evidence for it, the risks, and what would change the recommendation.

questions.hint: Sensitivity shows how robust the recommendation is.

items.title: L12: Explaining a decision to the public: choosing the best wording
items.source: GOV.UK: Style guide, A to Z and words to avoid; Content design: planning, writing and managing content
items.body:
The GOV.UK style guide helps writers choose wording that people understand at first reading. Several rules apply to decision letters and web pages.

Use "must" for an obligation set by law or policy, and avoid "should", which is unclear about whether the thing is required. "You must tell us within 28 days" is clearer than "You should tell us". Use "need to" where it is about what a person has to do to get something.

Put the thing the reader most needs first. If the decision is a refusal, the first line says so, with the reason following. Do not hide it behind a history. Write in the active voice: "We have decided to refuse your application" rather than "It has been decided that your application is to be refused". The active voice names who did what.

Turn abstract nouns back into verbs. "We carried out an assessment of your income" becomes "We assessed your income". Keep sentences short, aiming at an average of about 15 to 20 words, and keep one idea in each paragraph. Use "you" and "we", and contractions such as "we'll" where the tone is friendly.

Avoid words that sound impressive but say little. The style guide lists words to avoid, including "deliver" (for services or promises), "facilitate", "leverage", "robust", "tackling", "strengthen", "going forward", "key" (as in "key priorities") and "impact" as a verb. Say what you will actually do. Do not use Latin abbreviations such as "e.g." or "i.e." Write "for example" and "that is". Do not use "etc."

Use numerals and the % sign with a number: "5%". Write "per cent" only in text where %, a symbol, cannot be used. Explain any acronym the first time, and do not assume the reader knows it.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best uses "must"?

options.text: You should tell us within 28 days if your address changes.
You are advised to tell us within 28 days if your address changes.
You must tell us within 28 days if your address changes.
It is recommended that you tell us within 28 days if your address changes.

questions.hint: "Must" shows a requirement; "should" is unclear.

questions.prompt: A decision letter refuses an application. Where should the refusal go?

options.text: After a summary of the relevant law
In the final paragraph, after the background
In a leaflet attached to the letter
In the first sentence, followed by the reason

questions.hint: The reader should not have to hunt for the answer.

questions.prompt: Which version is in the active voice?

options.text: It has been decided that your application is to be refused.
We have decided to refuse your application.
Your application has been refused by the team.
Your application was not able to be accepted.

questions.hint: The active voice names who did what.

questions.prompt: Which rewrite turns the abstract noun back into a verb?

options.text: We carried out an assessment of your income.
An assessment of your income has been undertaken.
Your income was the subject of an assessment.
We assessed your income.

questions.hint: A nominalisation hides the action.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the words the style guide asks writers to avoid?

options.text: Facilitate
Help
Make
Show

questions.hint: Say what you will actually do.

questions.prompt: What should replace "e.g." in a public letter?

options.text: Such as per the above
For example
As follows
For instance, see below

questions.hint: Latin abbreviations are avoided.

questions.prompt: What should be done the first time an acronym appears?

options.text: Use it without any explanation, as readers will know it
Put the acronym in bold so that it stands out
Spell it out in full with the acronym after it
Explain it in an annex at the end only

questions.hint: Do not assume the reader knows it.

questions.prompt: Which sentence length is the guide's rough target for average sentences?

options.text: About 15 to 20 words
About 35 to 40 words
About 5 words
There is no target

questions.hint: Short sentences are easier to read.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the clearest way to give a percentage?

options.text: About 5% of cases are reviewed.
About five per cent. of cases are reviewed.
Roughly 5 percent of cases are reviewed.
Approximately five % of cases are reviewed.

questions.hint: Use numerals with the % sign.

questions.prompt: Which phrase shows vague, impressive-sounding language?

options.text: We will open three new offices by the end of June.
We will deliver a robust programme going forward.
We will reply to your letter within 10 working days.
We will send our decision to you by post.

questions.hint: It says little about what will actually happen.

items.title: L12: RAID logs: risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies
items.source: HM Government: Orange Book (management of risk); Government Functional Standard GovS 002: Project delivery
items.body:
A RAID log is a single list of Risks, Assumptions, Issues and Dependencies. It is used by project and programme teams, and managers read it to see what could knock delivery off course. Each type has a precise meaning.

A risk is something that might happen in future and would affect objectives. An issue is something that has already happened and needs managing now. When a risk occurs, it is closed as a risk and becomes an issue. An assumption is something taken to be true without proof, such as "the supplier will deliver by June". An assumption should be tested and given a date for confirmation, or it can become a risk. A dependency is something you need from another team or project, with a date, or something others need from you.

Each risk entry has a description (cause, event and effect), an owner, a score, a mitigation, and a review date. Scores are usually likelihood multiplied by impact, each rated on a scale such as 1 to 5. A risk with likelihood 3 and impact 5 scores 15. A risk with likelihood 4 and impact 3 scores 12, and likelihood 2 with impact 5 scores 10. A threshold, such as 15 or above, can trigger escalation. The score before mitigation is the inherent score. The score after the controls are in place is the residual score, which should be lower if the controls work.

Name one owner for each entry. Close an entry with the reason, such as "occurred and moved to issues" or "no longer applies", and keep the closed items for the record. Do not allow a log to become a list of generic worries. If the same risk never changes and no mitigation exists, the entry is not being managed.

questions.prompt: Which entry belongs in the issues column, not the risks column?

options.text: The supplier may fail to deliver the software
The supplier has failed to deliver the software
The supplier could be late if staff leave
The software might not integrate

questions.hint: An issue has already happened.

questions.prompt: What happens when a risk occurs?

options.text: It stays on the log as a risk, with a higher score
It is converted into an assumption
It is closed as a risk and logged as an issue
It is deleted from the log, as it is no longer a risk

questions.hint: It needs managing now.

questions.prompt: What is a RAID assumption?

options.text: A known fact that has been checked against evidence
A decision recorded by the programme board
A problem that has already happened
Something taken to be true without proof

questions.hint: It should be tested and dated.

questions.prompt: A risk has likelihood 3 and impact 5 on 1-5 scales. What is its score?
questions.hint: Likelihood multiplied by impact.

questions.prompt: Likelihood 4 and impact 3: what is the score?
With an escalation threshold of 15 or above, which risk is escalated?

options.text: Likelihood 4, impact 3
Likelihood 3, impact 5
Likelihood 2, impact 5
Likelihood 1, impact 5

questions.hint: Only 3 x 5 reaches 15.

questions.prompt: What is a residual risk score?

options.text: The score before any controls are applied
The highest score the risk has reached
The score allocated by the programme board
The score after the controls are in place

questions.hint: It should be lower than the inherent score.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a dependency?

options.text: The data feed may not arrive on time
The data feed has arrived late
The data feed is expected to be of good quality
The team needs the data feed from another department by 30 April

questions.hint: A dependency is something needed from another party, with a date.

questions.prompt: How many owners should each RAID entry have?

options.text: Two, to share responsibility
The whole team
One named owner
None until it is scored

questions.hint: Clear ownership drives action.

questions.prompt: What indicates that a risk is not really being managed?

options.text: It has a review date set for next month
It is scored by likelihood and impact
It is owned by a senior manager
It never changes and has no mitigation

questions.hint: A static entry with no action is just a worry.

items.title: L12: Controllers, joint controllers and processors
items.source: ICO: Controllers and processors; UK GDPR Articles 26, 28 and 33
items.body:
The UK GDPR gives different duties to controllers and processors. A controller decides why and how personal data is processed. A processor processes data on behalf of a controller and follows its instructions. The roles are about who decides, not about what the contract says: an organisation that decides its own purposes for the data is a controller, even if it is called a supplier.

When a controller uses a processor, Article 28 requires a written contract. It must set out the subject matter, duration, nature and purpose of the processing, the type of personal data and the categories of data subject. It must also require the processor to: act only on the controller's documented instructions; use a sub-processor only with the controller's authorisation, and keep the same obligations in place down the chain; help the controller respond to individuals' rights requests and to breaches; delete or return the data at the end of the contract; and allow audits and inspections.

If two or more organisations jointly decide purposes and means, they are joint controllers. Article 26 requires a transparent arrangement setting out who does what, particularly for individuals' rights and information, and the essence of it must be made available to individuals.

A processor must tell the controller of a breach without undue delay. The controller must notify the ICO within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach that is likely to risk individuals' rights and freedoms, unless the risk is unlikely. Contract terms should set the processor's notice period short enough to allow the controller to meet that limit.

A processor that starts to decide its own purposes for the data, for example using it for its own product, takes on the role of a controller for that processing and may be in breach.

questions.prompt: What mainly decides whether an organisation is a controller or a processor?

options.text: What the contract between the parties calls it
Whether it decides why and how the data is processed
Whether it is a private company or a public body
How much personal data it holds

questions.hint: The test is about decisions, not labels.

questions.prompt: Which article of the UK GDPR requires a written contract with a processor?

options.text: Article 5
Article 26
Article 33
Article 28

questions.hint: Article 28 deals with processors.

questions.prompt: Which is a required term of a processor contract?

options.text: The processor decides the purposes of use
The processor may use any sub-processor it chooses
The processor keeps the data indefinitely
The processor acts only on documented instructions

questions.hint: The controller directs the processing.

questions.prompt: When may a processor engage a sub-processor?

options.text: Only with the controller's authorisation
At any time without telling the controller
Only if it is in the UK
Only if the data is not special category

questions.hint: Authorisation and flow-down obligations are required.

questions.prompt: What must happen to personal data when the contract ends?

options.text: It is archived by the processor for future audit
It is deleted or returned, at the controller's choice
It is anonymised and kept for the processor's research
It is passed to the next supplier

questions.hint: The contract must provide for this.

questions.prompt: Two departments jointly decide the purposes and means of a data project. What are they?

options.text: Joint controllers, needing an Article 26 arrangement
Processor and sub-processor, bound by Article 28
Independent processors with separate contracts
Controller and data subject, under Article 15

questions.hint: They share responsibility.

questions.prompt: A supplier uses the data it holds for a client to train its own product. What is the effect?

options.text: It remains a processor, because the data came from the client
It becomes a joint controller with the client automatically
It acts as a controller for that use, and may be breaching the contract
It is in the clear, if the data is encrypted

questions.hint: Deciding its own purposes makes it a controller.

questions.prompt: Within what time must a controller notify the ICO of a notifiable breach?

options.text: 24 hours of the breach occurring
7 days of discovery
72 hours of becoming aware
One month of becoming aware

questions.hint: This is the Article 33 limit.

questions.prompt: Who must tell the controller about a breach affecting data the processor holds?

options.text: The ICO, at the processor's request
The processor, without undue delay
The data subject first
Nobody until the controller finds out

questions.hint: The controller's clock depends on prompt notice.

questions.prompt: Why should a contract set a short deadline for the processor to report a breach?

options.text: Because processors must notify the ICO themselves
So the controller can still meet its own 72-hour limit
So the processor can reduce what it charges
Because every breach must be fixed within 24 hours

questions.hint: The limit applies to the controller.

items.title: L12: Subject access requests: scope, third-party data and exemptions
items.source: ICO: Right of access; UK GDPR Article 15; Data Protection Act 2018, Schedule 2
items.body:
A subject access request (SAR) gives a person the right to a copy of their personal data and other information about the processing. It can be made in any form, including by email or on social media, and does not need to mention the law. Time starts when the request is received, or when you receive any ID or clarification you have reasonably asked for. The deadline is one calendar month, ending on the corresponding date in the next month. A request received on 15 January is due by 15 February. If there is no such date, as with a request received on 31 January, it falls on the last day of the following month, so 28 February in 2025. The time can be extended by up to two further months if the request is complex or the person has made a number of requests, and the person must be told within the first month.

The right is to personal data, not documents. You may provide the data in a new document, but it is often easier to supply copies with redactions. Fees cannot normally be charged. A request that is manifestly unfounded or excessive can be refused or a reasonable fee charged, but the bar is high.

Where the information also identifies another person, you must weigh competing interests. You do not have to disclose it unless the other person consents or it is reasonable to do so without consent. The rest of the data is still provided. Exemptions include legal professional privilege, confidential references given by the department, and management forecasting. Each is applied case by case and recorded, and the person is told of the right to complain to the ICO and to go to court.

questions.prompt: A SAR is received on 15 January. What is the usual deadline?

options.text: 14 February
1 March
15 April
15 February

questions.hint: One calendar month to the corresponding date.

questions.prompt: A SAR is received on 31 January 2025. By when must it be answered?

options.text: 31 March 2025
1 March 2025
28 February 2025
3 March 2025

questions.hint: There is no corresponding date, so it is the last day of the next month.

questions.prompt: How long can the time be extended for a complex request?

options.text: Up to one further month
Up to six months
Up to two further months
Indefinitely, if the department decides

questions.hint: The person must be told in the first month.

questions.prompt: What does a request need in order to count as a valid SAR?

options.text: It can come in any form and need not cite the law
It must cite Article 15 of the UK GDPR
It must be made in writing on the department's form
It must be addressed to the data protection officer

questions.hint: The law does not require a particular wording.

questions.prompt: The requester's right is to which of the following?

options.text: Every document in which their name appears
Copies of all internal discussions about their case
Access to the complete case file held on them
A copy of their personal data and information about the processing

questions.hint: It is about personal data, not documents.

questions.prompt: A letter also contains another person's details. What should be done first?

options.text: Withhold the whole letter to protect the other person
Send the letter unredacted, as the requester is entitled to it
Ask the requester to obtain the other person's consent
Weigh whether to disclose, considering consent and whether it is reasonable

questions.hint: The rest of the data is still provided.

questions.prompt: Which exemption can apply to a SAR?

options.text: Legal professional privilege
Embarrassment to the department
A heavy workload in the team
The age of the records

questions.hint: Exemptions are specific and recorded.

questions.prompt: What is the normal rule on fees for a SAR?

options.text: Nothing can normally be charged
A flat fee of £10 applies to every request
A fee of up to £50 applies for large searches
The department sets whatever fee it thinks right

questions.hint: A fee may be charged only for manifestly unfounded or excessive requests.

questions.prompt: What does the response also have to tell the person?

options.text: About the right to complain to the ICO and to go to court
Who else has made a request about them
Which manager handled the case
The department's budget for subject access work

questions.hint: The person's remedies must be set out.

questions.prompt: A team says it only needs to supply the documents, not the data. What is wrong with that?

options.text: Documents are always exempt from a subject access request
Documents are provided only if the requester asks for them
The right is to personal data, which may need extracting or redacting from documents
The right covers emails and no other type of record

questions.hint: Information about the person is what counts.

items.title: L12: Information assets and using AI notetakers
items.source: Cabinet Office: Government Functional Standard GovS 007 (Security) and information management guidance; ICO guidance on AI and data protection
items.body:
Departments keep an information asset register (IAR): a list of the important sets of information they hold, such as a case database or a shared drive of contracts. Each entry names an information asset owner (IAO), a senior person who is accountable for it, what the asset contains, how it is classified, who may access it, where it is stored, how long it is kept, and what the risks are. The senior information risk owner (SIRO), a board-level role, takes overall responsibility for information risk, and the IAOs report to them. Managers are expected to know which assets they use and to make sure changes, such as a new system or supplier, are recorded.

AI meeting tools that record, transcribe or summarise calls are now common. A transcript or summary of a meeting is a record and may contain personal data, so the usual rules apply. Use only a tool that your department has approved for the classification of the discussion. Tell participants that the meeting is being recorded and why, and do not use it for confidential personnel, security or legal matters unless the policy allows. Check the summary for errors before it is circulated: tools can mishear names, invent action owners or miss the decision.

Treat the output as a draft that a named person must check and agree. Store the approved version in the proper system, and delete the raw audio and transcripts in line with the retention schedule. A recording can be requested under FOI or a subject access request, so do not keep more than you need. Do not let a tool join a meeting uninvited with an external provider, and do not forward a transcript outside the department without checking.

questions.prompt: What is an information asset register?

options.text: A list of all staff who hold a security clearance
A register of every FOI request the department receives
A list of important sets of information with an owner, risks and handling details
A log of the software licences the department owns

questions.hint: It shows what is held and who is accountable.

questions.prompt: Who is accountable for an individual information asset?

options.text: The IT helpdesk
Any user of the asset
The information asset owner
The data protection officer alone

questions.hint: IAOs are senior people responsible for their assets.

questions.prompt: Which responsibility sits with the senior information risk owner?

options.text: Day-to-day running of the IT systems
Handling all FOI requests
Checking staff clearances
Overall responsibility for information risk at board level

questions.hint: IAOs report to the SIRO.

questions.prompt: A team introduces a new case system. What should its manager do?

options.text: Wait for the IAO to notice the change
Add it only when an audit asks for it
Make sure the system is recorded on the information asset register
Record it in the team's own rota instead

questions.hint: Changes must be reflected in the register.

questions.prompt: What is true of an AI-generated transcript of a meeting?

options.text: It is likely to be a record and may contain personal data
It is not a record, because a machine produced it
It is exempt from FOI, as it is only a draft
It can be kept for ever without a retention period

questions.hint: The same information rules apply.

questions.prompt: Before using an AI notetaker, what must be checked first?

options.text: That the tool is approved for the classification of the discussion
That the tool is free to use for the whole team
That all of the attendees speak clearly
That the tool is installed on a personal laptop

questions.hint: Approval depends on classification.

questions.prompt: Which meeting is least suitable for an AI notetaker unless policy allows it?

options.text: A team planning session about a public leaflet
A confidential discussion about a staff disciplinary case
A weekly update on a project timeline
A training session on a public-facing service

questions.hint: Sensitive personnel matters need extra care.

questions.prompt: What should happen to an AI-generated summary before it is circulated?

options.text: A named person checks and corrects it
It is sent immediately to speed things up
It is deleted without being read
It is sent only to external attendees

questions.hint: Tools can mishear names or invent action owners.

questions.prompt: What should be done with the raw recording once the approved record exists?

options.text: Keep it permanently in case it is needed later
Send a copy to every attendee to confirm the notes
Store it on a personal drive for backup
Delete it in line with the retention schedule

questions.hint: Do not keep more than you need.

questions.prompt: Why should participants be told that a meeting is being recorded?

options.text: Transparency about the processing is required and they can raise concerns
Recordings are only lawful if attendees pay for them
Each recording must be sent to the ICO for approval
It makes the transcript more accurate

questions.hint: People should know how their data is used.
